header:
Date: 2026-01-25 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42m
Redwood: Maya Chen (AE), Ethan Park (SE) | Customer: Priya Nair (CTO), Liam O'Connor (Lead Eng), Sara Bennett (PM)
summary: Introductory hosted API demo focusing on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, key generation parameters, retry/backoff strategies, and a lightweight implementation playbook for a 3-month pilot. Customer is conservative on latency and needs SOC2 and VPC options. Agreed to POC with benchmarks.
topics: console traces and per-token cost visibility
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we really appreciate you taking the time. This is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. With me is Ethan Park from our SE team.
[00:00:08] Priya Nair: Hi Maya hi Ethan, Priya here. We have Liam and Sara on our end — thanks.
[00:00:12] Ethan Park: Great, quick agenda, we'll do a 30 minute walkthrough of the hosted chat API, show streaming, param impacts, and retries; then 10–15 for specific infra and pilot questions. Sound good?
[00:00:20] Liam O'Connor: Yep, that sounds good. We're especially interested in latency numbers and how retries affect cost.
[00:00:28] Maya Chen: Perfect. One quick note — do you have any compliance or network constraints? I remember you mentioned SOC2 and VPC earlier in the intake form.
[00:00:36] Priya Nair: Yes SOC2 is a must. Also we prefer VPC peering or a private deployment for anything PII adjacent. For the initial pilot we could start with hosted if the data stays ephemeral.
[00:00:46] Ethan Park: Totally, that's the common path. Our hosted API supports ephemeral payloads and we can enable data redaction; for deeper control we can discuss Redwood Private or Dedicated. I'll show some of the console controls that help with retention and audit logs.
[00:01:02] Sara Bennett: And can you show the console trace for a streaming call? We want to see how tokens map to latency and cost.
[00:01:08] Ethan Park: Yeah, absolutely. I'll share my screen — bear with me while I open the demo sandbox.
[00:01:32] Ethan Park: (screen) Ok so this is the sandbox, top-left is the model selection. For this demo I'm using a 4k-context open model that Redwood catalogs as "r-adapt-4k" — sometimes the catalog names get munged in the transcript — sorry if I say weird things.
[00:01:48] Priya Nair: No worries.
[00:01:52] Ethan Park: Starting a streaming chat request now. You can see partial tokens arrive as SSE events; front-end gets them incrementally. The latency per first token here is around 120ms in our sandbox region, but in production it depends on routing and the model variant.
[00:02:14] Liam O'Connor: When you say first token latency, is that cold start or steady state?
[00:02:19] Ethan Park: Good call — that's a warm path number. Cold starts can be 500ms to a couple seconds depending on spin-up; we do pre-warming for steady traffic and Dedicated gives much lower variance.
[00:02:34] Maya Chen: Also worth calling out the difference between per-token latency vs total generation latency — they correlate but batching changes the math.
[00:02:42] Priya Nair: How does batching affect costs?
[00:02:45] Ethan Park: Batching improves throughput and lowers unit cost by amortizing kernel work across requests. In hosted mode automatic continuous batching will group similar sequence lengths — but it can add a small micro-batch delay. You can tune target latency in the Console Optimize tab to balance.
[00:03:05] Sara Bennett: So for our use case — short confirmations and a few follow-ups — we'd favor lower tail latency, right?
[00:03:11] Ethan Park: Yes if you need sub-200ms tails you might prefer a smaller batch window and sometimes a Dedicated pool. Hosted is still viable if you tune the params and use smaller model variants.
[00:03:23] Liam O'Connor: Can you demo parameter effects — like temperature and top_p — and how that changes token counts?
[00:03:29] Ethan Park: Sure. I'll run the same prompt twice — once with temperature 0.2 and top_p 0.9, then with temperature 0.9.
[00:03:42] [00:03:42] Ethan Park: (typing) First run: temp 0.2 — output is concise, tokens 48.
[00:03:50] [00:03:50] Ethan Park: Second run: temp 0.9 — output more verbose, tokens 86. So cost roughly doubles for that prompt.
[00:03:59] Priya Nair: That's a big swing. We need predictable unit economics.
[00:04:03] Maya Chen: Totally — that's where our Optimize recommendations help. The Optimize tab will analyze a sample prompt set and suggest temperature/top_p and quantization/model families to hit your cost target while preserving quality. I can show an example later.
[00:04:18] Liam O'Connor: How do retries work? We saw in earlier vendors that naive retries blew up our bill.
[00:04:24] Ethan Park: Great question. Redwood recommends idempotency keys for user-level requests; for generation we expose retry tokens and a recommended backoff policy. The Console has a retry policy editor where you can set max retries, jittered backoff, and fallbacks to cheaper model variants.
[00:04:44] Sara Bennett: Can fallback swap to a quantized model automatically?
[00:04:48] Ethan Park: Yes — you can configure a fallback chain. Example: r-adapt-4k -> r-adapt-4k-8bit -> r-adapt-2k-8bit. If higher tier is overloaded it'll try the next one. We also emit trace events so you can see when fallbacks happen.
[00:05:01] Priya Nair: Do those fallbacks change the API shape or require client changes?
[00:05:06] Ethan Park: No client change typically. The endpoint stays the same; the routing is policy-driven on the server side. You might want to expose a header to the client to indicate model variant for debugging.
[00:05:18] Liam O'Connor: And streaming with fallback — does it stream partials from the fallback model?
[00:05:23] Ethan Park: Yes, once the fallback is selected we stream from that variant. There can be a small discontinuity if the initial model timed out and fallback kicks in — we recommend idempotency and sequence markers so the client can stitch events or request a fresh generation.
[00:05:40] Maya Chen: Quick note on metrics: in Console you can get token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency percentile, and a trace for each request that shows batching, kernel time, and queue wait.
[00:05:53] Priya Nair: Can we hook our APM into those traces?
[00:05:58] Ethan Park: Yes, we provide tracing hooks and an OpenTelemetry-compatible export. You can correlate Redwood traces with your service traces.
[00:06:06] Sara Bennett: Ok show us a failure mode — like a rate limit or kernel OOM — what's the customer experience?
[00:06:12] Ethan Park: If you hit a rate limit you'll get a 429 with Retry-After header; for OOMs we try graceful fallbacks and return a 503 if nothing matches. Our automatic fallbacks reduce user-facing errors in most cases.
[00:06:28] Priya Nair: How are credentials and keys handled in hosted mode? We need KMS integration.
[00:06:34] Maya Chen: In hosted we integrate with customer KMS via customer-managed keys in some tiers; we also support HSM integrations for Private deployments. For the pilot we can use managed keys and present the SOC2 controls.
[00:06:52] Liam O'Connor: You mentioned persistent KV cache earlier in the intake — how does that play with chat context?
[00:06:58] Ethan Park: Redwood uses a KV cache to store long-running attention states — it's optional. For short chats we typically keep the KV in-memory per session; for large contexts we spill to a fast key-value store. In transcripts sometimes the word comes out as KV "cash" in the speech-to-text — that was a running joke in the product docs.
[00:07:19] Sara Bennett: (laughs) noted. For the pilot, our main concerns: 95th percentile latency under 350ms for short prompts, predictable cost per session, and SOC2 evidence.
[00:07:29] Maya Chen: Understood. Those are reasonable. For 95th under 350ms we'll recommend a smaller batch window, a lightweight model variant, and reserved Dedicated capacity if traffic is spiky. We'll include cost estimates for both hosted tuning and Dedicated monthly reserved pools.
[00:07:46] Priya Nair: How invasive is the client change? We have a React front-end.
[00:07:50] Ethan Park: Minimal. For streaming we recommend the SSE approach or WebSocket. We have SDK snippets for React that handle reconnection and idempotency tokens. For fallbacks the SDK surfaces a model variant header and a simple retry helper.
[00:08:06] Liam O'Connor: Can you show the SDK snippet?
[00:08:09] Ethan Park: Sure — (scrolls) here's the JS snippet. You set an idempotency key, open the stream, and handle partials. There's also a helper for automatic reconnection with exponential backoff.
[00:08:32] Sara Bennett: Any notes on token counting for billing? Do you bill input + output?
[00:08:36] Maya Chen: Yes input + output tokens are billed; however Optimize can recommend prompt compaction and prefix caching to reduce repeated tokens. We'll share a sample spreadsheet that shows how prompt engineering affects monthly costs.
[00:08:52] Priya Nair: Can we run a small benchmark with 1k sample prompts?
[00:08:56] Maya Chen: Absolutely. Ethan will prep a benchmark harness and a template for you to drop in prompts. We usually run latency and throughput tests across variants: hosted baseline, hosted tuned, Dedicated reserved pool.
[00:09:12] Ethan Park: I'll outline the test steps: 1) run warmup at low concurrency; 2) measure P50/P95/P99 over sustained load; 3) test fallback triggers by artificially limiting capacity; 4) capture Console traces and token costing.
[00:09:30] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. What about rate limits and quotas for the pilot?
[00:09:35] Maya Chen: For pilot we'll set soft quotas and monitoring, and can raise limits as needed. For Dedicated there's an SLA and predictable throughput; hosted quotas are adjustable.
[00:09:46] Priya Nair: Is there any self-serve step to enable VPC peering?
[00:09:50] Ethan Park: For hosted we do a guided setup. For Private deployments it's more involved — we have an infra checklist. We'll attach that checklist in the next email.
[00:10:03] Sara Bennett: Ok, could you summarize the pilot proposal?
[00:10:07] Maya Chen: Sure — proposed pilot: 3 months, start with hosted tuned variant, run benchmark with your 1k prompts, if results are within agreed latency/cost targets we move to either Dedicated reserved pool or Private deployment depending on compliance needs. We'll provide security docs, pricing, and a test harness.
[00:10:24] Priya Nair: What would success criteria look like?
[00:10:27] Maya Chen: Agreed metrics: P95 < 350ms for short prompts, token cost per session under X (we'll estimate), no unaddressed SOC2 items, and integration work < 2 engineer-weeks.
[00:10:41] Liam O'Connor: Two engineer weeks OK. That helps.
[00:10:44] Ethan Park: Quick demo follow-up — I'm going to show the Console Optimize tab which suggests batching and quantization. (screen) Here you see recommendations and an estimated cost delta. It also surfaces risky prompts that expand tokens.
[00:11:05] Sara Bennett: Nice. Can these recommendations be automated?
[00:11:09] Ethan Park: You can apply recommended profiles to a route — e.g., apply a quantization profile and a cache TTL. We also have a scheduler to roll changes during off-peak windows.
[00:11:22] Priya Nair: Any gotchas we should be aware of?
[00:11:25] Maya Chen: A few: 1) too aggressive quantization can affect hallucinations; 2) naive retries increase cost if requests aren't idempotent; 3) very wide fallback chains can add surprising latency. We'll document those in the playbook.
[00:11:43] Liam O'Connor: On the security pack, will you include pen test results?
[00:11:47] Maya Chen: We can share third-party assessment summaries and SOC2 reports. For pen tests we can share scopes and remediation summaries where permissible.
[00:11:57] Priya Nair: Great.
[00:12:00] Maya Chen: Ok we're coming up on time, let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[00:12:04] Maya Chen: Recap — demo of streaming partials, param effects on token usage, retry/backoff strategy and fallbacks, Console traces and Optimize recommendations, and a proposed 3-month pilot starting with a hosted tuned variant.
[00:12:19] Maya Chen: Next steps: I'll send security pack and pricing; Ethan will send benchmark harness and test plan; Liam will share sample prompts and confirm stakeholders.
[00:12:28] Priya Nair: Sounds good to me. Thanks Maya and Ethan.
[00:12:31] Sara Bennett: Thanks everyone.
[00:12:33] Liam O'Connor: Thanks.
[00:12:40] Ethan Park: Thanks all. We'll follow up in email with the attachments.
[00:12:44] Maya Chen: Bye!
[00:12:48] [call continues briefly off-record on scheduling but not transcribed]
[00:42:00] [end of recording]
